A Martin County judge ruled that a man charged with fatally stabbing a 73-year-old woman in a Stuart neighborhood is incompetent to stand trial, according to the State Attorney's Office. WATCH WPTV'S PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: Kersten Francilus, 25, was examined by two doctors and determined to be incompetent during a hearing on Aug. He has been remanded to a state mental hospital for restoration to competency before his case can proceed. Francilus faces premeditated first-degree murder charges in the April 2025 stabbing death of Joyce Ellen Thompson Adams in the Southwood community near Stuart. The Martin County Sheriff's Office arrest affidavit reveals the attack was far more brutal than initially reported. While investigators previously said Adams was stabbed approximately 16 to 17 times, they now believe she was stabbed more than 50 times. "Unfortunately, it's even worse than what I described the other day," Sheriff John Budensiek said. According to the affidavit, the first responding deputy arrived at the intersection of Southeast Black Oak Lane and Woods Edge Trail and witnessed Francilus stabbing Adams in the neck and back. Francilus dropped the knife and complied with commands to get on the ground when ordered by deputies at gunpoint. First responders transported Adams to the Cleveland Clinic South Emergency Room, where she was pronounced dead. Before the fatal stabbing, multiple residents reported a man matching Francilus' description walking through the Southwood neighborhood, approaching homes and asking about a nearby bank. Callers noted he appeared "out of it." "Yeah, he was knocking on doors, and most, I guess, everybody you know, just kept their door closed," neighbors Peter Burke and Lori Soo said. The affidavit reveals one resident told investigators the man came to her house asking for a bank. When she opened the door, he attempted to step inside, but she shut the door and alerted her husband. Sheriff Budensiek said Francilus specifically targeted women, asking whether their husbands were home, and approached two children in an open garage. "He asked multiple ladies if their husbands were home. All of which responded yes and closed the door," Budensiek said. "We have two kids that were in an open garage door where he asked them if the kids' parents were home and they turned around and — thankfully — ran inside and shut the door. This could have been a lot worse." This tragedy highlights ongoing concerns about mental health resources and intervention in Florida communities. The case underscores the critical importance of mental health treatment compliance and the challenges families face when loved ones refuse medication. Investigators spoke with Francilus' mother, who confirmed the serrated knife used in the attack came from their home. She told detectives she usually stored the knives above the microwave to hide them from her son. The mother also revealed her son had not taken his prescribed medication since February 2025. "He was on types of psychotropic medications for psychological problems," Budensiek said. "He was off the meds just because he didn't want to take them." The Martin County Sheriff's Office said Francilus had two prior encounters with law enforcement in 2025. One involved the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office and resulted in Francilus being Baker Acted. In September 2025, Francilus' mother called the Martin County Sheriff's Office to report her son was hearing voices. "The voices telling him to go here, go there," Budensiek said. "Our deputies got there, asked him if he was suicidal, 'no,' 'Do you want to hurt anyone?' 'No,' so at that point we didn't have enough to Baker Act him." Budensiek added that Francilus told deputies he had admitted himself into a mental health facility at Coral Shores shortly before that interaction, but investigators are still working to confirm that claim. During an interview with investigators, Francilus admitted to leaving his residence and said he "did what I did." When asked to describe Adams, Francilus said she was Jewish. However, the affidavit shows investigators spoke with Adams' daughter, who confirmed her mother was not Jewish. When asked if anything about her mother could lead someone to think she was Jewish, the daughter provided a brief response: "Possibly her appearance." Budensiek said nothing currently indicates Francilus was antisemitic, but detectives are working to determine whether that belief played a role in why Adams was targeted. A neighbor who wished to remain anonymous said he had spoken with Francilus before the stabbing and thought he seemed like he "wasn't all there" but was talking normally. He then heard screams and found Adams covered in blood, recognizable only by her shoes he had seen her wearing around the neighborhood. The neighbor tried to pull Francilus away but said Francilus was too heavy and did not appear to notice him. Francilus stopped only when deputies arrived and ordered him to the ground at gunpoint. Another neighbor said the situation was terrible but that at least Adams "is with her husband now," referring to her husband, who passed away 10 to 15 years prior. "So we don't know of any motive," Budensiek said. "At this point, we don't know of any nexus between the victim and the suspect. We simply know that we've had a horrendous crime that's taken place in this neighborhood." Paige O'Donnell has pleaded not guilty to 72 charges stemming from what the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast calls the worst animal hoarding case in its history, while legally surrendering the 36 Border Collies rescued from her Palm City home for adoption.WATCH PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW:According to Martin County court records, O'Donnell hired an attorney and posted a surety bond following her not guilty plea. The legal surrender clears the path for the rescued dogs to find new homes after undergoing medical evaluations and rehabilitation.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast confirmed O'Donnell's surrender of the dogs to WPTV, saying staff will complete thorough medical testing and evaluations before placement decisions. Potential adopters will receive clear information about any long-term medical needs the animals may have.The shelter will prepare the dogs for spay/neuter services, microchipping and vaccinations on a phased schedule alongside other animals in their care. Adoption applications are available on the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast's Facebook page, along with applications for 501(c)(3) rescue groups.The shelter is asking the public not to call about the Border Collies at this time to keep phone lines available for urgent shelter needs and services. All applicants will undergo extensive vetting to ensure appropriate matches between dogs and families.This case highlights the growing problem of animal hoarding in Florida and has prompted legislative action, including a push for mandatory dog breeder registries. The successful rescue and rehabilitation of these 36 Border Collies demonstrates how communities can respond to animal neglect while providing pathways for recovery and adoption.The dogs were rescued from O'Donnell's hoarded Palm City home earlier this month after a WPTV investigation helped renew the Martin County Sheriff's Office probe into the case. Deputies found the animals living in deplorable conditions, with fur matted with feces and debris.Court documents show O'Donnell exhibited deceptive behavior during the investigation, according to law enforcement, blaming strong odors on "missed trash collection" and "old seafood."The rescued Border Collies underwent what shelter staff call "medical grooming," a process involving carefully shaving severely matted fur while checking for injuries and infections underneath."We shaved 9 pounds off of one dog filled with feces and urine," said Sarah Fisher, spokesperson for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast.Fisher previously told WPTV that some dogs arrived with metal and glass fragments trapped in their fur. During the initial rescue, investigators found "lots of pieces of metal — rusted metal, sharp metal — that have been stuck in their fur, along with shards of glass," according to Fisher.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast says many of the rescued animals are already beginning to heal. Cesar Perea, associate vice president of rescue for American Humane Society, said the emotional and physical recovery process for animals often begins quickly once they are removed from dangerous conditions."As soon as you start providing care, you immediately start to see the animal's personality come out," Perea said. "When they were in that situation, they were completely shut down."Perea said trauma in rescued animals can appear as emotional shutdown, inactivity and fear, but he has seen dramatic turnarounds in many hoarding cases across the country."Within two weeks, you wouldn't even recognize that animal," Perea said. "They start getting a little more active and joyful. They start behaving like the pets that they're meant to be."Perea said animal hoarding can still qualify as criminal neglect under Florida law when animals are denied proper veterinary care, food or safe living conditions. He said communities should watch for several warning signs that animal hoarding may be occurring nearby."The smell will probably be your first indicator," Perea said. "If you see a lot of animals, more animals than you usually see people having as pets, that's also a big indicator."The case has prompted legislative action from State Rep. Meg Weinberger, R-Palm Beach Gardens, who is pushing for a mandatory dog breeder registry in Florida following the Palm City rescue.Perea said the situation can escalate when people feel compassion for animals but lack the resources to properly care for them."It becomes overwhelming very quickly when people feel that compassion to want to help animals, but then they don't have the resources or the ability to continue to manage and provide a level of care that's acceptable," Perea said.The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast is encouraging the public to adopt or foster available animals while the rescued Border Collies continue receiving treatment and rehabilitation. The shelter is also asking for donations to its emergency medical fund or through its Amazon Wish List.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A disturbing social media trend featuring a menacing version of the beloved Dr. Seuss character The Cat in the Hat is prompting warnings from school districts and law enforcement agencies nationwide. The trend includes videos and images of the character lurking outside homes and schools, and some containing threats. On the Treasure Coast, the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office said threats to schools there have so far been non-credible, but they’re sounding the alarm to students and parents. "Talk to your kids, make sure you're checking their social media, make sure you’re involved in what they're posting. And be friends with them and their accounts. So you know what's happening and what they're posting on social media," said Jaime Alberti, the director of school safety and emergency operations for the School District of Indian River County. Some of the images of the character appear to be generated with artificial intelligence. And though many of them are intended to be just memes or jokes, law enforcement officials said some people are taking it to the next level, including threatening language targeted at specific schools and communities. "When one kid thinks maybe [it’s] a joke, somebody else may be interpreting it not as a joke. And obviously context matters and everything when you post it online. So a lot of the folks that are reading this online are getting scared, and they're calling the police and they're calling in the Fortify Florida tip line to report, hey, I'm seeing this online. This is a concern," Alberti said. The School District of Indian River County said it has received two of these threats, one at Vero Beach Middle School and another at Sebastian River Middle School. The sheriff’s office said both are non-credible. The principal of Vero Beach High School also sent out a voicemail warning to parents. Administrators said students could face consequences if they are found to have issued a threat. "If it's specific, a specific threat on someone, they could be charged criminal charges. And if not, they would also face school discipline referrals against the code of student conduct," Alberti said. Administrators are urging parents to frequently monitor their children’s social media accounts. The Jim Brandon Equestrian Center has been granted a one-year reprieve, as Palm Beach County Commissioners gave a majority direction on Thursday to continue funding the public park through the next fiscal year. The 5-2 decision during the first of two budget hearings delays, for now, the controversial proposal to privatize the facility. The vote must be finalized at the next budget meeting on Sept. 15.Palm Beach County officials considered privatizing the public park to cut costs, a move that has sparked fierce opposition from the local equestrian community. The county says it spends $750,000 annually to maintain the facility, an expense it may not be able to afford amid potential property tax reforms.A Push from the PodiumThe effort to save the park's public funding was led by Commissioner Joel Flores, whose district includes the equestrian center. Hours before the meeting, Flores toured the facility and met with members of the Palm Beach Posse and other riders to understand the park's vital role in the community.He brought that perspective to the commission chambers."This kinda blindsided the community," Flores said during the meeting. "What I would love this board to do is to help me to find a way to fund them through the next year."His advocacy resulted in a majority of the board agreeing to direct staff to find the necessary funds.A Temporary SolutionWhile supporters celebrated the decision, Flores warned that the fight to keep the park public is not over. He cited the looming threat of future budget shortfalls if a proposed state constitutional amendment on property taxes passes."We may be able to push this for another year," Flores said during his park tour earlier in the day. "If the Amendment Three happens, I want to be clear, I don't think there is any other option but to go to a P3 (Public-Private Partnership)."The Vote and What's NextWPTV reporter Michael Hoffman said Commissioners Woodward and Marino indicated no on the measure, while Commissioners Baxter, Flores, Weiss, Sachs and Powell indicated yes. It was a "majority direction," not a vote persay. Commissioners Woodwars and Marino indicated their opposition, citing concerns over using county reserves and the impact on other programs that have already faced cuts.The commission will take a final, binding vote on the entire county budget, including the funding for the equestrian center, at its second public hearing on Sept.

Lucie man is accused of striking the mother of his children with a vehicle and driving several houses down the street while she was on the hood, according to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. Brandon Isaiah Martin, 24, was arrested Sept. 2 on an outstanding warrant charging him with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon. The warrant identifies a motor vehicle as the alleged weapon. The charge stems from an April 28, 2025, incident on 26th Court Southwest in Vero Beach, court records show. Deputies said the woman went to the home after a friend told her Martin was there removing property. The woman told deputies Martin was attempting to leave with their two children. The pair had joint custody but no formal custody documentation, according to the probable cause affidavit. As the woman was placing one of the children into another vehicle, Martin allegedly drove a silver Kia Soul toward her and struck her, causing her to land on the hood, deputies wrote. The woman told deputies Martin continued driving with her on the hood for about four or five houses. She said she heard him threaten to kill her, according to the affidavit. The vehicle stopped after Martin’s mother, who was in the front passenger seat, put it in neutral, deputies said. The woman was able to get off the hood and told deputies she feared for her life. A witness told deputies she saw Martin drive toward the woman, strike her and continue down the street with the woman still on the hood. Deputies documented abrasions to the woman’s knees, records show. See also: Florida woman cleared under 'Stand Your Ground' after deadly Walmart parking spot fight A judge approved the warrant May 5, 2025, and set Martin’s bond at $50,000. The order also prohibits him from contacting the woman and requires him to stay specified distances away from her, her home, workplace and vehicle. Deputies served Martin with the warrant at a Vero Beach address on Sept. Jail records show he later posted bond.

A narcotics investigation led to the arrest of a convicted felon after detectives say they found 33 pounds of marijuana, more than $150,000 in cash, and multiple firearms at a Fort Pierce home. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Special Investigations Division detectives, assisted by the agency’s SWAT Team and the U.S. Marshals Service , executed a narcotics-related search warrant Wednesday morning at a residence in the 700 block of Cedar Place. Investigators arrested 59-year-old Stacy Tyrner of Fort Pierce without incident. During the search, detectives seized approximately 33 pounds of marijuana and more than $150,000 in cash, along with multiple firearms. Investigators also found boxes of ammunition matching the calibers of the firearms, additional gun parts and components, drug paraphernalia, packaging materials, a currency counter, and other items they say were consistent with the sale and distribution of narcotics. According to the sheriff’s office, Tyrner is a convicted felon and is prohibited from possessing firearms. See also: Byron Donalds holds Q&A with voters in Delray Beach Tyrner was charged with: Sale/delivery of a controlled substance, stemming from a warrant arrest Trafficking in marijuana Possession of a firearm by a convicted felon Possession of drug paraphernalia Drugs destroy lives and fuel crime, and we will not allow criminals to profit from that destruction, Sheriff Richard Del Toro said. Del Toro praised the Special Investigations Division, SWAT Team, and U.S. Marshals Service for their work in removing what he described as drugs, illegal firearms, and illicit cash from the community. This is another step toward our goal of making St. Lucie County the safest county in Florida, Del Toro said.

Lucie County Republican Executive Committee Chairman Kenneth Ford Nail was arrested in Martin County after deputies said he harvested saw palmetto berries from public parks without a permit authorizing the locations. A Martin County sheriff ’s deputy stopped Nail’s gray Kia Soul on Aug. 25 near Southwest Murphy Road and Southwest Island Way in Palm City after a records check showed the temporary tag was unassigned and had expired five days earlier, according to a probable cause affidavit. The deputy said he saw a bundle of saw palmetto berries in the car and cutting shears on the front passenger seat. Nail later told deputies he had picked berries at parks in Jensen Beach and Palm City and had more berries in the rear hatch area, the affidavit states. Nail told deputies he had a Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services permit for his mother’s property, but asked whether he could also pick berries on public land, according to the report. Deputies said the permit applied only to the address listed on it. He was arrested on a charge of harvesting palmetto berries without a permit or landowner permission. Deputies photographed the berries and returned them to nature, the affidavit states. The affidavit says Nail was held without bond because he was already out on bond in a case alleging the introduction of contraband into a correctional facility. RELATED STORIES Indian River man accused of hauling 150 pounds of illegally harvested saw palmetto berries 4 arrested after Florida deputies say they illegally harvested 200 lbs of palmetto berries Nail, 57, was chairman of the St. Lucie County Republican Executive Committee in 2023 and early 2024. He was among local Republicans who publicly called for then-Gov. Ron DeSantis’ appointee, Sheriff Keith Pearson, to resign over an FDLE investigation into the 2020 sheriff’s race. In April 2025, Nail was arrested at Okeechobee Correctional Institution after deputies alleged that legal documents he was attempting to serve on an inmate concealed cellphones, chargers, and alprazolam, according to an Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office narrative. Nail denied knowing the contraband was inside the documents, the report said.

Lucie woman is among seven people charged in an alleged tax refund fraud scheme that sought more than $57 million from the IRS , according to the U.S. A superseding indictment unsealed Wednesday charges Sherita Chandler of Port St. Lucie, along with defendants from Idaho, Illinois, California and Georgia, with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, making false claims and money laundering. Federal prosecutors allege the group worked from 2023 through 2024 to prepare and submit false individual and trust tax returns, along with more than 100 fictitious financial instruments, to claim refunds from the IRS. The defendants allegedly sought more than $57 million in refunds and received more than $8 million in taxpayer money, the Justice Department said. Chandler; Andrea and Kent Shannon of Kuna, Idaho; and Monika Skinger of Chicago had previously been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, according to prosecutors. The Shannons also face additional allegations involving wire fraud, false claims and money laundering, including claims that they bought luxury vehicles with fraudulently obtained refunds. See also: Therapist intern arrested over alleged sexual relationship with client at facility The investigation is being handled by IRS Criminal Investigation. A conspiracy to commit wire fraud charge carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. An indictment is an allegation, and all defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast has begun placing Border Collies rescued from a Palm City hoarding case into new homes, marking a major milestone in the dogs’ recovery . The shelter said it has slowly started facilitating adoptions and shared photos from one of the first successful placements. To protect the adopters’ privacy and give the dogs time to adjust, the Humane Society will not immediately identify the new owners or arrange media follow-ups. Shelter staff will stay in regular contact with adopters, conduct follow-up checks and provide support during the transition, the organization said. Training classes also will be available for dogs needing extra attention or help adjusting to life in a home. The adoptions come less than a month after Martin County deputies and Animal Services removed 36 Border Collies from a home on Southwest Alligator Street in Palm City. Authorities said the dogs were found in deplorable conditions, with feces, urine-soaked materials and debris throughout the home. The dogs were later legally surrendered to the Humane Society, allowing the shelter to move ahead with medical care, behavioral evaluations and the adoption process. CBS12 previously reported many of the dogs arrived frightened, matted and covered in dried waste. Shelter workers provided grooming, baths, vaccinations and veterinary treatment for issues including skin and eye infections, body sores and intestinal parasites. Some dogs may require continuing veterinary care, and shelter staff have said they are carefully screening potential homes because the animals need patient adopters familiar with the breed’s needs. Paige O’Donnell , 62, faces 72 charges in the case 36 third-degree felony counts involving alleged animal cruelty and 36 misdemeanor counts alleging animals were kept without sufficient exercise and air. O’Donnell recently posted a $270,000 surety bond and was released from jail, according to Martin County court records. A judge ordered that she have no pets while out on bond. She has pleaded not guilty. The Humane Society said it is encouraged by the first placements and will continue working to ensure each Border Collie is safely matched with an appropriate home. The shelter’s Name Your Price adoption special for dogs and cats older than 1 remains available until further notice. More information is available at hstc1.org .

A Vero Beach woman is being held without bond on two sexual battery charges after an Internet Crimes Against Children investigation in Michigan led deputies to her Indian River County home, according to an arrest affidavit. Lisette Zamarripa, 28, was arrested Sept. 3 by the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office . She is charged with two counts of sexual battery and one count of electronic transmission of child sexual abuse material. Zamarripa’s arraignment is scheduled for 9 a.m. According to the affidavit, Michigan State Police received a National Center for Missing and Exploited Children cybertip involving alleged child sexual abuse material associated with a Kik account. Investigators obtained a search warrant for the account and found images and videos allegedly showing an adult woman engaging in sexual acts with two children, a 1-year-old girl and a 2-year-old boy, both her biological children. DCF took custody of the children. Michigan investigators identified the woman as Zamarripa after comparing material from the account with her Facebook profile, the affidavit states. Michigan investigators also served a search warrant on Zamarriapa's boyfriend, Kenneth Conkle, where he admitted to directing and recording the abuse. He confessed to separately abusing his own 1-year-old daughter. Indian River County deputies went to Zamarripa’s Vero Beach home after investigators believed the children could be in immediate danger. A family member confirmed Zamarripa was inside with her two children, according to the affidavit. Deputies said Zamarripa came outside with the children and was separated from them. After being advised of her rights, she allegedly admitted that she committed sexual acts involving both children during a FaceTime call with their biological father, who lives in Michigan. He faces charges in Michigan including child sexual battery, four counts of production of aggravated CSAM, and five counts of using a computer to commit a crime. Florida charges against Conkle are pending. The affidavit says Zamarripa told detectives the acts had been discussed with the father beforehand and that she livestreamed at least one incident for him to view. Investigators said she initially denied one allegation but later identified the children in sanitized images shown to her and admitted the conduct described in the evidence. See also: Florida woman cleared under 'Stand Your Ground' after deadly Walmart parking spot fight Deputies seized Zamarripa’s cellphone, which she allegedly said was used to record the material. She is being held with no bond on the two sexual battery charges. Bond was set at $500,000, cash or surety, on the electronic transmission charge. The affidavit states prosecutors intended to seek a grand jury indictment on two counts of capital sexual battery because of the children’s ages.

Linn Stewart, a 75-year-old resident of Indian River County, starts her day at 2:30 a.m., driving through the dark to feed her colony of stray cats, a routine that has become central to her life. "You're up at 2:30 every morning?" she was asked. "Umm hmm, a lot of times I'm out at 2:30 every morning," Stewart said. While most people are still asleep, Stewart is already hard at work caring for animals that have become like family to her. "I've only required four hours of sleep since I was little. I drove my parents crazy," she said. Her love for animals has been a lifelong passion. "I've always loved animals. I would bring home anything and everything," Stewart said. "Once I got involved with (For the Love of) Paws, I realized that there were so many cats running around that I would just take care of them." After feeding the cats, Stewart volunteers 60 hours a week at For the Love of Paws in Fellsmere, a sanctuary for pets left behind by senior citizens who can no longer care for them. The organization also operates a pet food pantry, providing free pet food to food banks, veterans, and senior citizen organizations. "We have a cat group and a dog group, and we put them on the tables, and we cut open the bags and dump them in bins, and then what we do is we transfer them to 4-pound bags," Stewart said. Stewart said the sanctuary provides more than just food. We provide medical sometimes. We get the donations and provide flea medications if we have it. It's just something that is really needed and appreciated," she said. Having lost her parents at the age of 30 and with little family nearby, Stewart said giving back is what keeps her going. I would be finding something to do," she said. Her compassion extends beyond cats and dogs. "I've stopped and rescued tortoises, turtles. I stopped one time last week, there was a coyote that had gotten hit. I realized it was a coyote. I still called to have somebody pick it up," she said. Stewart’s dedication has not gone unnoticed. "Love for Paws is part of your family. Well, at Guardians, we live that as well. We'd like to welcome you to the Guardians family, and thanks for all you do. You're rooted in your community, and we love to celebrate that. So congratulations, $525.25 goes to you," she was told. For Stewart, her work is a source of purpose and joy. "It keeps me going," she said. "I'll probably just disappear one day, but other than that, I have no health issues right now. Knock on wood, but this keeps me going because I have love for the animals." If you live in Indian River County or are just passing through, don’t be surprised if you see Stewart lending a hand to the helpless. Lucie woman is among seven people charged in an alleged tax refund fraud scheme that sought more than $57 million from the IRS , according to the U.S. A superseding indictment unsealed Wednesday charges Sherita Chandler of Port St. Lucie, along with defendants from Idaho, Illinois, California and Georgia, with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, making false claims and money laundering. Federal prosecutors allege the group worked from 2023 through 2024 to prepare and submit false individual and trust tax returns, along with more than 100 fictitious financial instruments, to claim refunds from the IRS. The defendants allegedly sought more than $57 million in refunds and received more than $8 million in taxpayer money, the Justice Department said. Chandler; Andrea and Kent Shannon of Kuna, Idaho; and Monika Skinger of Chicago had previously been charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud, according to prosecutors. The Shannons also face additional allegations involving wire fraud, false claims and money laundering, including claims that they bought luxury vehicles with fraudulently obtained refunds. See also: Therapist intern arrested over alleged sexual relationship with client at facility The investigation is being handled by IRS Criminal Investigation. A conspiracy to commit wire fraud charge carries a maximum penalty of 20 years in prison. An indictment is an allegation, and all defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

A threatening AI-Cat in the Hat post targeted Vero Beach High School amid a viral nationwide wave of similar school threats, but deputies say it is not credible. There are no credible threats to Indian River County schools or students at this time, the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office said in an announcement on Facebook . Deputies are investigating the trend, monitoring social media activity and coordinating with the School District of Indian River County to help ensure campus safety. The sheriff’s office said any student found to have participated in the activity could face discipline under the Code of Student Conduct and potentially criminal charges. See also: Indiantown residents demand action as flooding persists CBS12 is also working to obtain an email sent to parents about the situation. The warning comes as law enforcement agencies nationwide respond to a viral trend involving AI-generated images of the Cat from the 2003 live-action Cat in the Hat movie starring Mike Myers. USA TODAY reported that the trend, initially described as a prank intended to scare people online, has prompted some school districts to increase security or cancel classes out of an abundance of caution. Authorities in communities including Louisville, Kentucky, Falfurrias, Texas, and Hanover County, Virginia, have also issued warnings about posts referencing schools or individual students. In some cases, the posts have used the Cat in the Hat character alongside threatening language, according to law enforcement agencies cited by USA TODAY. The IRCSO is urging anyone who sees threatening content involving local schools or students to report it to law enforcement rather than sharing it. The sheriff’s office emphasized that while the current posts reviewed locally have not been deemed credible, all threats involving school safety are being taken seriously.

A Vero Beach man was arrested and is being held on a $1 million bond after creating and distributing AI-generated sexually explicit images of women without consent. Officers with the Vero Beach Police Department say 37-year-old Peter Solomon Ruma took photos from social media and other online sources to create some of the altered images. Ruma's home and electronic devices were searched by investigators on Wednesday, and evidence was found connecting back to the creation and distribution of the AI-generated images. See also: FAA seeks permanent flight restrictions near Mar-a-Lago, keeping rules around DJT airport After the investigation, an arrest warrant was obtained, and Ruma is currently facing eight charges stemming from incidents occurring between June and August 2026 relating to one female victim, including: 3 counts of creating altered sexual depictions 3 counts of promoting those depictions 1 count of sexual cyber harassment 1 count of stalking Police have identified several additional potential victims who have not been identified or may not know images of them were created or shared. Investigators also believe Ruma may have engaged in this conduct for years. Court records show Ruma has a prior criminal history in Indian River County. In 2007, he was arrested on charges that included burglary and sex battery on a physically impaired person. In 2009, he was arrested on a burglary charge and was later sentenced to the Florida Department of Corrections. The case comes amid growing concerns nationwide over AI-generated deepfakes, which can be used to create realistic-looking but fabricated sexual images of real people. Federal officials recently launched TakeItDown.FTC.gov, a resource that allows victims to report nonconsensual intimate images and seek their removal from online platforms. Investigators are publicly urging anyone who believes they may have been victimized, or who has received, viewed, or has information regarding the altered or explicit images, to contact the Vero Beach Police Department . The investigation is still ongoing, and additional charges could be filed.

Lucie police have announced an operational pause on license plate readers in the city, saying the pause will limit the technology to circumstances where there is an immediate threat to human life. There are currently 126 license plate readers throughout the city. Residents are divided on the technology.WATCH BELOW: Port St. Lucie police pause usage of license plate readers"I think they're great. I really do," neighbor Joseph Hamm said.However, neighbor Peter Schmitt sees it differently."I think they should be illegal," Schmitt said. "It's a privacy invasion."WPTV reporter Tyler Hatfield sat down with Port St Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk, who said the pause is about responding to community concerns."My position from the beginning has been very simple. You need to respond when the community expresses concern. You need to approach it with an open mind," Niemczyk said.He said the goal of the pause is to find a path forward that preserves public trust."The whole idea of our pause is to figure out how we can re-establish regular use while maintaining the trust of the community," Niemczyk said.Niemczyk also moved to address misconceptions about how the technology works. He said the readers are not using biometrics or facial recognition, but instead take pictures of the rear of vehicles. He also said the technology is not used for any traffic enforcement."There's no red light enforcement there. There's no speeding enforcement. That's not what they're used for," Niemczyk said.Niemczyk said the technology has delivered measurable results, including a 17% reduction in auto burglaries and a reduction in traveling crime."I've got an extremely valuable tool that not only is reducing crime, but saving lives," Niemczyk said.Niemczyk said he wants lawmakers in Tallahassee to get answers from manufacturers like Flock about data retention and work with legislators to provide usage guidelines that protect both the community and officers, and establish consequences for misuse."It's made us more effective. It's been an incredible tool, but at what cost?" said Niemczyk. "If it costs me the trust of the community, I've got to figure out how to balance that. Lucie County Republican Executive Committee Chairman Kenneth Ford Nail was arrested in Martin County after deputies said he harvested saw palmetto berries from public parks without a permit authorizing the locations. A Martin County sheriff ’s deputy stopped Nail’s gray Kia Soul on Aug. 25 near Southwest Murphy Road and Southwest Island Way in Palm City after a records check showed the temporary tag was unassigned and had expired five days earlier, according to a probable cause affidavit. The deputy said he saw a bundle of saw palmetto berries in the car and cutting shears on the front passenger seat. Nail later told deputies he had picked berries at parks in Jensen Beach and Palm City and had more berries in the rear hatch area, the affidavit states. Nail told deputies he had a Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services permit for his mother’s property, but asked whether he could also pick berries on public land, according to the report. Deputies said the permit applied only to the address listed on it. He was arrested on a charge of harvesting palmetto berries without a permit or landowner permission. Deputies photographed the berries and returned them to nature, the affidavit states. The affidavit says Nail was held without bond because he was already out on bond in a case alleging the introduction of contraband into a correctional facility. He was among local Republicans who publicly called for then-Gov. Ron DeSantis’ appointee, Sheriff Keith Pearson, to resign over an FDLE investigation into the 2020 sheriff’s race. In April 2025, Nail was arrested at Okeechobee Correctional Institution after deputies alleged that legal documents he was attempting to serve on an inmate concealed cellphones, chargers, and alprazolam, according to an Okeechobee County Sheriff’s Office narrative. Nail denied knowing the contraband was inside the documents, the report said.

Lucie man is accused of striking the mother of his children with a vehicle and driving several houses down the street while she was on the hood, according to the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office. Brandon Isaiah Martin, 24, was arrested Sept. 2 on an outstanding warrant charging him with aggravated battery with a deadly weapon. The warrant identifies a motor vehicle as the alleged weapon. The charge stems from an April 28, 2025, incident on 26th Court Southwest in Vero Beach, court records show. Deputies said the woman went to the home after a friend told her Martin was there removing property. The woman told deputies Martin was attempting to leave with their two children. The pair had joint custody but no formal custody documentation, according to the probable cause affidavit. As the woman was placing one of the children into another vehicle, Martin allegedly drove a silver Kia Soul toward her and struck her, causing her to land on the hood, deputies wrote. The woman told deputies Martin continued driving with her on the hood for about four or five houses. She said she heard him threaten to kill her, according to the affidavit. The vehicle stopped after Martin’s mother, who was in the front passenger seat, put it in neutral, deputies said. The woman was able to get off the hood and told deputies she feared for her life. A witness told deputies she saw Martin drive toward the woman, strike her and continue down the street with the woman still on the hood. Deputies documented abrasions to the woman’s knees, records show. The order also prohibits him from contacting the woman and requires him to stay specified distances away from her, her home, workplace and vehicle. Deputies served Martin with the warrant at a Vero Beach address on Sept. Jail records show he later posted bond.

A 28-year-old Vero Beach woman and her 38-year-old boyfriend in Michigan are facing charges of child sex abuse, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and Van Buren County Sheriff’s Office said Friday. A joint Internet Crimes Against Children investigation involving the Michigan State Police, Indian River County Sheriff’s Office in Florida and the Van Buren County Sheriff’s Office in southwest Michigan has resulted in the arrests of the man and woman following an investigation into the alleged sexual abuse of children, and the production and transmission of child sexual abuse material. The investigation began after law enforcement received a cybertip from the National Center for Missing Exploited Children regarding suspected child sexual abuse material transmitted through the online messaging platform Kik, the Van Buren agency said. Investigators obtained legal process for associated online accounts and recovered images, videos and communications that identified an adult female in Florida and an adult male in Michigan as persons of interest. "This investigation reflects the coordinated efforts of local, state, and federal law enforcement partners working across state lines to identify offenders, preserve digital evidence, and protect children from exploitation," the Van Buren County Sheriff’s Office said in a news release. What happened in Vero Beach On Thursday, IRCSO’s internet crimes against children detectives were contacted by the Michigan State Police, the sheriff's office in Vero Beach said. Investigators there had found images and videos on a Kik account showing a woman sexually abusing two young children. Detectives identified the woman as Lisette Zamarripa and responded to her home, where they located and safely removed the two victims, a 1-year-old girl and a 2-year-old boy, both her biological children. The home's location is redacted in the arrest report. The Department of Children and Families took custody of the children. Zamarripa admitted to sexually abusing the children and recording it during a video call at the request of her boyfriend, Kenneth Conkle, who was watching from Michigan, the sheriff's office said. She was located and arrested roughly 2.5 hours after detectives received the initial tip and charged with two counts of sexual battery and transmission of child sexual abuse material. Zamarripa is being held in the county jail on no bond. The arraignment is set for Oct. "Protecting children is always the top priority of the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office," the IRCSO said. "This kind of abuse is absolutely unacceptable and will never be tolerated in our county. We’re proud of our detectives, who acted quickly to get these children out of a dangerous situation, and grateful to investigators in Michigan for their partnership on this case, even from states away." What happened in Michigan The Van Buren County Sheriff’s Office served a search warrant at Conkle’s home, where he admitted to directing and recording the abuse. He confessed to separately abusing his own 1-year-old daughter. Detectives were contacted and requested to immediately secure potential digital evidence from him before it could be destroyed or deleted. Investigators obtained a search warrant for the suspect’s residence. Because information indicated firearms were present at the residence, the search warrant was treated as a high-risk operation. Members of the Van Buren County Sheriff's Office were able to execute the search warrant without incident. During the search, detectives assigned to the Van Buren County Sheriff’s Office Computer Crimes Unit seized a cellular telephone, two computers, and a tablet believed to contain evidence of child sexual abuse material. The devices will undergo forensic examination as the investigation continues. Also during the investigation, detectives developed evidence and obtained statements indicating the male suspect allegedly sexually abused the 1-year-old victim. The male suspect was arrested and is in the Van Buren County Jail. He faces charges including first-degree criminal sexual conduct and multiple counts related to the manufacture of aggravated child sexually abusive material. Additional charges may be authorized as the investigation and forensic examination of the seized devices continue. He is due in court on Sept. Florida charges against Conkle are pending. He is in the jail on $2 million bond. The seized digital devices will undergo forensic examination for additional evidence, and investigators continue to work with their state and federal ICAC partners. "This investigation demonstrates the importance of agencies working together across jurisdictions when crimes against children are identified," Sheriff Daniel Abbott in Michigan said. "The investigation remains ongoing. The seized digital devices will undergo forensic examination for additional evidence, and investigators continue to work with their state and federal ICAC partners. "Our detectives and patrol deputies acted quickly to secure evidence and protect these children. We are grateful for the cooperation and dedication of all of our ICAC partners who worked together to bring these suspects to justice and, most importantly, ensure the safety of these children.” Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25 Get the latest news updates with the WPBF 25 News app.

Deputies confirmed that a body found in the mangroves near the House of Refuge is that of Michael Anthony Debevec, who was reported missing last week. Investigators with the Martin County Sheriff's Office say they found Debevec's body Tuesday after an extensive search of the area around Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island. Detectives reported that they have not found any apparent signs of foul play. The Medical Examiner has not yet determined Debevec's cause of death. The search began after a Good Samaritan found a wallet Saturday belonging to Debevec. The person went to Debevec's home in an attempt to return it, prompting his family to report him missing. Investigators later found Debevec's vehicle at Chastain Beach, more than two miles from where his body was ultimately discovered. See also: Viral 'Cat in the Hat' threat targets Vero Beach High School; deemed not credible Sheriff John Budensiek said investigators determined Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. 27, and parked at Chastain Beach. Phone records showed Debevec's phone was in use Friday morning and moving between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge, according to investigators. On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree. His computer was inside the backpack. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to the body. The sheriff's office said Debevec's family has been notified of his death. The Martin County Sheriff's Office thanked the community members who shared information about Debevec and helped with the search.

Deputies with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office are investigating a shootout between two teenagers, ages 15 and 17, in a residential neighborhood Wednesday night. Neighbors said detectives were in the area throughout the night gathering evidence, and everyone is relieved no one was injured. Julio Pitts, a resident in the area, said he was sitting in his living room when the shots rang out. "The car had to have been here, and he had to shoot like that, boom, boom, boom, boom," Pitts said. Authorities released a photo of one of the weapons believed to have been used in the shooting. Kevin Jaworski said the weapon was recovered after the 17-year-old suspect was taken into custody Thursday morning. "So, my first thing that comes to my mind is, where did he get it? This is a short-barreled pistol, a rifle that he was shooting in the middle of the street," Jaworski said. The incident occurred in the 1100 block of 12th Court Southwest at around 7:30 p.m. Deputies responded to multiple 911 calls and found bullet casings at the scene. A nearby home and vehicle had been struck by gunfire. Investigators said they obtained video showing the two teenagers shooting at each other in the roadway. "Yes, yes, between the 17-year-old and the 15-year-old, they were actively shooting at each other in the middle of the street," Jaworski said. Authorities believe the shootout stemmed from an ongoing feud between the two teens. While the cause of the feud remains unclear, officials said the incident appears to be isolated. "This was between those two juveniles, so there’s no threat to the community at this point, but it is inherently dangerous to be shooting firearms in the middle of the street because, like I said, a car was hit, a house was hit, and if anybody was in those, they could have very well easily been hurt," Jaworski said. Pitts expressed frustration over the incident and called for action to prevent similar events in the future. "I say crime watch, but when everybody sees something wrong, they got to say something," Pitts said. The case remains under investigation, and authorities are urging anyone with information to contact detectives. A Vero Beach man, Peter Ruma, is accused of using artificial intelligence to turn social media photos into pornography, raising concerns about the dangers of posting images on social media. Greg Schiller, CEO of the Boca Raton-based nonprofit Child Rescue Coalition, said this type of activity is becoming increasingly common. "Everyone's got to be concerned about what people are potentially doing with their images," Schiller said. The Child Rescue Coalition provides technology to help law enforcement track down child sex predators worldwide. While Ruma's case does not involve children, Schiller said the accusations serve as a reminder that predators can use a simple photo of a child to create harmful content. "The increased number of cyber tips that are related to AI-generated child sexual abuse material has gone through the roof," Schiller said. He added that this issue applies to adults as well, warning that a photo posted on social media today could be altered into pornography by tomorrow. "I think people need to be conscious of that, know what's happening, and before they post a picture of their child especially, let's think about the idea that people can now use those images," Schiller said. Schiller said the easiest way to protect yourself and your family is to stop posting on social media. However, he also said there are ways to continue posting while maintaining as much security as possible. Schiller advised keeping social media settings private and limiting who can see your posts. At the same time, he also emphasized that nothing is truly safe on the internet. "I think that's the most important message. Just think before you act on these things and understand that there might be repercussions," Schiller said. As for Ruma, he is currently charged with altering photos of one woman, but police believe there may be more victims and additional charges could follow. Deputies confirmed that a body found in the mangroves near the House of Refuge is that of Michael Anthony Debevec, who was reported missing last week. Investigators with the Martin County Sheriff's Office say they found Debevec's body Tuesday after an extensive search of the area around Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island. Detectives reported that they have not found any apparent signs of foul play. The Medical Examiner has not yet determined Debevec's cause of death. The search began after a Good Samaritan found a wallet Saturday belonging to Debevec. The person went to Debevec's home in an attempt to return it, prompting his family to report him missing. Investigators later found Debevec's vehicle at Chastain Beach, more than two miles from where his body was ultimately discovered. See also: Viral 'Cat in the Hat' threat targets Vero Beach High School; deemed not credible Sheriff John Budensiek said investigators determined Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. 27, and parked at Chastain Beach. Phone records showed Debevec's phone was in use Friday morning and moving between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge, according to investigators. On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree. His computer was inside the backpack. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to the body. The sheriff's office said Debevec's family has been notified of his death. The Martin County Sheriff's Office thanked the community members who shared information about Debevec and helped with the search.

A Vero Beach man, Peter Ruma, is accused of using artificial intelligence to turn social media photos into pornography, raising concerns about the dangers of posting images on social media. Greg Schiller, CEO of the Boca Raton-based nonprofit Child Rescue Coalition, said this type of activity is becoming increasingly common. "Everyone's got to be concerned about what people are potentially doing with their images," Schiller said. The Child Rescue Coalition provides technology to help law enforcement track down child sex predators worldwide. While Ruma's case does not involve children, Schiller said the accusations serve as a reminder that predators can use a simple photo of a child to create harmful content. "The increased number of cyber tips that are related to AI-generated child sexual abuse material has gone through the roof," Schiller said. He added that this issue applies to adults as well, warning that a photo posted on social media today could be altered into pornography by tomorrow. "I think people need to be conscious of that, know what's happening, and before they post a picture of their child especially, let's think about the idea that people can now use those images," Schiller said. Schiller said the easiest way to protect yourself and your family is to stop posting on social media. However, he also said there are ways to continue posting while maintaining as much security as possible. Schiller advised keeping social media settings private and limiting who can see your posts. At the same time, he also emphasized that nothing is truly safe on the internet. "I think that's the most important message. Just think before you act on these things and understand that there might be repercussions," Schiller said. As for Ruma, he is currently charged with altering photos of one woman, but police believe there may be more victims and additional charges could follow. (AP) — LSU coach Lane Kiffin’s chances of fielding former NFL players improved Thursday night when a Louisiana judge issued a preliminary injunction against the NCAA in a high-profile eligibility case. East Baton Rouge Parish Judge William Jorden issued his ruling the night before LSU was due to submit its 105-man roster to the Southeastern Conference, which last week announced heavy potential punishment for football and basketball teams that bring in ex-pros. The ruling clears the way for LSU to list some former NFL players on its roster. How many games they might be eligible to play remains to be seen as the matter continues working its way through the courts. “It’s not about coach Kiffin. It’s about treating these kids fairly,” said Tony Clayton, an attorney for the athletes. “Today, justice was served. And justice was serve to the SEC. It was served like a cold cup of gumbo. And that judge forced him to eat it.” Jorden said he considered sanctions against the SEC and the NCAA but ruled he was not ready to issue any at this time. Jorden's decision followed a nearly nine-hour hearing in a courtroom near the LSU campus during which athlete after athlete took the stand to explain why they should be allowed to return to play college sports after turning pro. The commissioner of the powerful SEC argued against them, and the league doubled down by filing a lawsuit against the school in federal court. That lawsuit could now become the SEC's best chance at preventing former pros from playing this season. The hearing was attended by Louisiana attorney general Liz Murrill, who filed a brief in the case on behalf of the athletes. While she did not make any arguments in court, she spoke after the ruling and referred to the SEC's federal lawsuit against LSU as “legal garbage.” “It was an attempt at a collateral attack on this judge that it was a message to say that, ‘If you rule against us here, that we’re going to try and go to federal court in Alabama and get a ruling that is a federal ruling that binds you,’” Murrill said. “I don’t think this judge was impressed by that threat.” The courtroom confrontation came just two days before 11th-ranked LSU opens the season at home against Clemson. Jorden scheduled the hearing over his temporary injunction preventing the NCAA from barring former pros or fifth-year college athletes, a stance reiterated by the SEC and other Power Four conferences in potential punishments adopted last week. Former NFL players testify about modest pay in pros Former New Orleans Saints defensive lineman Zxavian Harris and former Cleveland Browns tight end Dae’Quan Wright, two players who now expect to suit up for LSU within weeks, sat next to each other in the gallery as the hearing began and both took the stand to say they would have not tried to turn pro had they known they might get another year in college. Harris and Wright said they each earned about $1 million in college. Harris said he was paid just $190 in travel expenses by the Saints and spent all of his time with the club rehabbing a foot injury. Wright said he was paid a $25,000 signing bonus by Philadelphia before his brief time with the Browns and would gladly pay that back for the chance to play for LSU. While both former Mississippi players were unsure how soon they might make their LSU debut, they said after the hearing that they expect to play when the Tigers visit Ole Miss on Sept. Two LSU soccer players, Jazmin Ferguson and Jocelyn Ollivierre, won earlier court orders and have already played this season. Ferguson testified that she was paid $4,500 by a USL team, but ended her contract and paid the money back in hopes of clearing the way to play for the Tigers again. Two LSU softball players also testified. The athletes testified after SEC Commissioner Greg Sankey was on the stand for more than two hours, defending the league’s authority to enforce its longstanding rules barring former pros from returning to play at its 16 member schools, and enforce newly outlined fines and suspensions against programs and coaches. He said school presidents and chancellors felt that they needed to establish a line between professional and college sports and that there needed to be ways to hold schools accountable. “The line between professional sports and college sports needs to be maintained,” Sankey testified, adding that the league was concerned about incoming athletes being displaced from limited roster spots. As he spoke, the SEC filed the federal lawsuit in Alabama against LSU and its leadership, alleging the school had “waged a deliberate and coordinated campaign to recruit professional athletes” in defiance of league rules. The court filing against one of the league’s founding members in 1933 seeks an injunction barring LSU from violating the SEC’s First Amendment rights by forcing it to “associate with conduct that is contrary to the conference’s purpose and mission.” Legal experts said the filing was a backup in case the SEC lost in state court. Outside the courthouse in Baton Rouge, Clayton said: “I got a problem with that. I mean, you go around, you can file this suit in any state. You go to our nemesis: Alabama. So, that lets you know what the commissioner is all about.” Questioning of Sankey turns sharp In questioning Sankey, attorneys for the athletes cited numerous examples of when SEC eligibility rules align with NCAA rules, suggesting the potential of collusion. They questioned why league members met last week to adopt stiff penalties for the very actions addressed in the Louisiana state court’s temporary injunction against the NCAA. The attorneys also asked why the SEC singled out players who signed contracts with specific U.S.-based leagues — the NFL, NBA and WNBA — but not overseas pro leagues or women’s pro soccer leagues. When Sankey tried to qualify an answer about whether the SEC had previously punished a school for adding a player with previous pro experience, Clayton said, “I didn’t ask how to build a clock. I’m just asking what time it is.” Sankey acknowledged that there had previously been no such punishment, but that it had been considered against Alabama last basketball season when the Crimson Tide briefly added a former G League player. Players going to court has become common The players in question also include former Denver Broncos defensive back Blake Cotton, who like Harris and Wright is hoping to join LSU and Kiffin. Wright, who played for Kiffin last season at Ole Miss, started practicing at LSU this week, too late to be eligible for Saturday’s home opener against Clemson under the NCAA’s required seven days of practice. Harris has committed to LSU, while Cotton, who played at Utah last fall, has been recruited by Kiffin. All three are among a host of athletes who’ve argued in lawsuits around the country that they are unfairly being denied an opportunity to spend a fifth year in college under newly adopted NCAA rules allowing for five full years of competition. In all, the NCAA says there are approximately 450 athlete plaintiffs seeking additional eligibility through litigation, with some 300 of them winning the ability to play at least for now. NCAA attorney Taylor Askew said the number of disputes actually strengthens the argument that the NCAA is trying to enforce rules fairly. “Was it applied inconsistently? Absolutely not,” Askew said. It's consistency.” The athletes in the case who signed pro contracts have argued they did so only because current rules that would have allowed them another college season weren’t adopted until after their decisions to leave for the chance to make an NFL roster. The SEC contends the question before the judge should be a narrow one regarding whether the conference “can enforce and require its member institutions to comply with SEC rules.” The SEC’s proposed punishments include significant fines, up to half-season suspensions for coaches and member universities’ loss of voting privileges on league business matters. Sankey provided an affidavit stating that SEC university presidents had voted 15-0 in favor of the new rules, with LSU’s Wade Rousse abstaining. The fight over eligibility between schools and their own conferences and the NCAA has simmered for months and spilled into politics. Jeff Landry posted on X to attorneys general in Georgia and South Carolina that “calling them ‘NFL players’ is at best disingenuous, and at worst intentionally deceptive.” “They are not professional football players circling back after years in the NFL,” Landry wrote. “They are college players who were told, by the NCAA, that they were done.

(AP) — The Missouri Supreme Court has unanimously blocked new congressional districts backed by President Donald Trump from being used in the November election and ordered a statewide vote on whether to uphold or reject the new map. The decision Thursday marks a rare setback for Republicans in a national redistricting battle. Republicans had hoped Missouri’s new congressional boundaries could help them win an additional seat and hold onto their slim House majority in the midterms. Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway, a Republican, said she would immediately appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, asserting that the decision “has thrust our state into a full‑fledged constitutional crisis.” Missouri’s new districts were used in the August primaries. But the state Supreme Court said they cannot be used in the November general election — or ever again, unless voters first uphold the new districts passed by the Republican-led Legislature. The court ruled that the new districts were effectively placed on hold in December, when opponents submitted over 300,000 petition signatures seeking to put the map to a vote of the people. Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins waited until primary election day in August to reject the petition. He asserted that the referendum process cannot be used for congressional redistricting. A lower court agreed, but the Supreme Court overturned Hoskins’ decision. “The referendum petition was legal, sufficient, and timely, and the secretary incorrectly concluded otherwise,” the court said in its ruling. The legislation containing the new districts “did not go into effect and will not go into effect unless and until approved by the voters.” As a result, the congressional map adopted after the 2020 census “remains in full force and effect for the November 2026 general election.” Hanaway, whose office represented Hoskins, called the ruling an unprecedented violation of federal law. Mike Kehoe, who proposed the new congressional map to lawmakers. “Never before in American history has a court overturned a congressional map after a primary and before a general election," Hanaway said in a statement. Court ruling hinged on referendum rights The Missouri Constitution does not specifically say a referendum petition can be used for a congressional redistricting law passed by the Legislature. But the Supreme Court ruled that a constitutional provision allowing a referendum on “any act” of the Legislature encompasses congressional redistricting. It rejected assertions from Hanaway's office that federal law prohibits referendum petitions on congressional redistricting. “This is what democracy looks like," said Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, which sponsored the referendum petition. "The people of Missouri demanded a voice, and the court just confirmed what we’ve been saying all along. People, not politicians, will have the final say.” Hoskins, acknowledging the loss, vowed to continue “the war to preserve our constitutional republic." The ruling, which capped a year of political maneuvering and legal wrangling, was one of two to go against Republican officials Thursday. The Supreme Court also ruled that Hoskins had wrongly rejected a petition for a ballot proposal making it difficult for politicians to change measures enacted by voters through citizen initiatives. The court also ordered that measure to be placed on the November ballot. Missouri redistricting targeted longtime Kansas City lawmaker Missouri currently has six Republicans and two Democrats in the U.S. After Trump urged Republicans to redraw congressional districts to their advantage, Kehoe called lawmakers into a special session last year to dramatically reconfigure the 5th Congressional District, held by Democrat Emanuel Cleaver. Cleaver, who was unopposed in the August primary, has carried the Kansas City-based district with at least 60% of the vote in each of the past two elections. Rick Brattin won an August primary in the reshaped 5th Congressional District, which had been stretched eastward to include rural Republican areas. About 59% of the district's voters were new under the revised map, according to an Associated Press estimate. Cleaver had not posted campaign signs in many of the new rural areas, explaining that he was waiting for the Missouri Supreme Court’s decision. But he had vowed to continue his reelection campaign regardless of the outcome. “Despite the cynical and deeply shameful attempt to silence many of our neighbors, the people fought back and won,” Cleaver said in a social media post Thursday. Brattin, a Marine veteran and founding member of the conservative Missouri Freedom Caucus in the state Legislature, said the decision disenfranchises thousands of primary voters who now will be shifted to different districts with candidates they didn’t get to choose. The court “handed Democrats a decision they desperately needed in their effort to help national Democrats retake the U.S. House of Representatives," Brattin said in a statement. Redistricting battle spread to over a quarter of states Congressional districts typically are redrawn at the start of each decade, based on new census data. But Trump’s quest for a midterm election advantage triggered an unusual mid-decade redistricting battle that spread to more than a dozen states — and triggered a dozen lawsuits in Missouri alone. The Missouri Supreme Court ruling was one of only a few nationally to go against Republicans' redistricting plans. Prior to its latest ruling, Missouri’s top court already had rejected claims that the special session was illegal, mid-decade redistricting isn’t allowed and the new districts aren’t compact enough. After the Supreme Court heard arguments Wednesday, a couple hundred people chanted “Let us vote!” while rallying outside the courthouse. Grant Christensen, of Jefferson City, said he had signed the referendum petition to put the map to a vote. “Gerrymandering is the same as voter suppression,” Christensen said. "Cutting up districts in order to steer them to vote one way or the other is not fair.”

Vero Beach police say they believe there are additional victims and expect more charges against a man accused of creating and sharing AI-generated sexually explicit images of women without their consent. Police Chief David Currey said Thursday that the current eight charges against 37-year-old Peter Solomon Ruma involve one adult female victim. Ruma is being held at the Indian River County Jail on $1 million bond. Ruma is charged with three counts of creating an altered sexual depiction, three counts of promoting an altered sexual depiction, one count of sexual cyber harassment and one count of cyberstalking. Investigators said the victim came forward after discovering her image had been altered. Detectives searched Ruma’s home and seized two phones, Currey said, and a forensic review of the devices produced evidence that advanced the investigation. Police said Ruma allegedly used photographs of real women including images from social media and other publicly available online sources to make the altered sexual images. A person does not have to have sent an intimate photo to be victimized, police said. Currey said investigators have identified several other women who may have been subjected to similar conduct, some of whom may not know their images were obtained, manipulated or shared. Police also said the investigation uncovered complaints and law enforcement contacts involving unwanted communications and similar behavior dating back several years. See also: Palm Beach County employee fired following alleged 'Heil Hitler' remark, Nazi salute Ruma is employed as a Lyft driver and Uber Eats driver, police said. Currey stressed that investigators have not alleged criminal conduct occurred while Ruma was working for either service, but released the information as they seek potential victims or people with concerning interactions involving him. Police believe Ruma acted alone, though Currey said that could change as the investigation continues. Anyone who believes they may have been victimized, received altered or sexually explicit images from Ruma, or has information for detectives is asked to contact Vero Beach police Detective Greg Matakaitis at 772-978-4665.

A Martin County judge ruled that a man charged with fatally stabbing a 73-year-old woman in a Stuart neighborhood is incompetent to stand trial, according to the State Attorney's Office. WATCH WPTV'S PREVIOUS COVERAGE BELOW: Kersten Francilus, 25, was examined by two doctors and determined to be incompetent during a hearing on Aug. He has been remanded to a state mental hospital for restoration to competency before his case can proceed. Francilus faces premeditated first-degree murder charges in the April 2025 stabbing death of Joyce Ellen Thompson Adams in the Southwood community near Stuart. The Martin County Sheriff's Office arrest affidavit reveals the attack was far more brutal than initially reported. While investigators previously said Adams was stabbed approximately 16 to 17 times, they now believe she was stabbed more than 50 times. "Unfortunately, it's even worse than what I described the other day," Sheriff John Budensiek said. According to the affidavit, the first responding deputy arrived at the intersection of Southeast Black Oak Lane and Woods Edge Trail and witnessed Francilus stabbing Adams in the neck and back. Francilus dropped the knife and complied with commands to get on the ground when ordered by deputies at gunpoint. First responders transported Adams to the Cleveland Clinic South Emergency Room, where she was pronounced dead. Before the fatal stabbing, multiple residents reported a man matching Francilus' description walking through the Southwood neighborhood, approaching homes and asking about a nearby bank. Callers noted he appeared "out of it." "Yeah, he was knocking on doors, and most, I guess, everybody you know, just kept their door closed," neighbors Peter Burke and Lori Soo said. The affidavit reveals one resident told investigators the man came to her house asking for a bank. When she opened the door, he attempted to step inside, but she shut the door and alerted her husband. Sheriff Budensiek said Francilus specifically targeted women, asking whether their husbands were home, and approached two children in an open garage. "He asked multiple ladies if their husbands were home. All of which responded yes and closed the door," Budensiek said. "We have two kids that were in an open garage door where he asked them if the kids' parents were home and they turned around and — thankfully — ran inside and shut the door. This could have been a lot worse." This tragedy highlights ongoing concerns about mental health resources and intervention in Florida communities. The case underscores the critical importance of mental health treatment compliance and the challenges families face when loved ones refuse medication. Investigators spoke with Francilus' mother, who confirmed the serrated knife used in the attack came from their home. She told detectives she usually stored the knives above the microwave to hide them from her son. The mother also revealed her son had not taken his prescribed medication since February 2025. "He was on types of psychotropic medications for psychological problems," Budensiek said. "He was off the meds just because he didn't want to take them." The Martin County Sheriff's Office said Francilus had two prior encounters with law enforcement in 2025. One involved the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office and resulted in Francilus being Baker Acted. In September 2025, Francilus' mother called the Martin County Sheriff's Office to report her son was hearing voices. "The voices telling him to go here, go there," Budensiek said. "Our deputies got there, asked him if he was suicidal, 'no,' 'Do you want to hurt anyone?' 'No,' so at that point we didn't have enough to Baker Act him." Budensiek added that Francilus told deputies he had admitted himself into a mental health facility at Coral Shores shortly before that interaction, but investigators are still working to confirm that claim. During an interview with investigators, Francilus admitted to leaving his residence and said he "did what I did." When asked to describe Adams, Francilus said she was Jewish. However, the affidavit shows investigators spoke with Adams' daughter, who confirmed her mother was not Jewish. When asked if anything about her mother could lead someone to think she was Jewish, the daughter provided a brief response: "Possibly her appearance." Budensiek said nothing currently indicates Francilus was antisemitic, but detectives are working to determine whether that belief played a role in why Adams was targeted. A neighbor who wished to remain anonymous said he had spoken with Francilus before the stabbing and thought he seemed like he "wasn't all there" but was talking normally. He then heard screams and found Adams covered in blood, recognizable only by her shoes he had seen her wearing around the neighborhood. The neighbor tried to pull Francilus away but said Francilus was too heavy and did not appear to notice him. Francilus stopped only when deputies arrived and ordered him to the ground at gunpoint. Another neighbor said the situation was terrible but that at least Adams "is with her husband now," referring to her husband, who passed away 10 to 15 years prior. "So we don't know of any motive," Budensiek said. "At this point, we don't know of any nexus between the victim and the suspect. We simply know that we've had a horrendous crime that's taken place in this neighborhood."
